# Wheeler and OpenSSF Contributors, finding and fixing software vulnerabilities using AI

**Source:** David A. Wheeler and OpenSSF Contributors, *Finding and Fixing Software Vulnerabilities Using AI: A Guide for Developers*, OpenSSF Best Practices and AI/ML working groups; `Finding.md` in ossf/wg-best-practices-os-developers at commit 82590814 (2026-10-05). The guide is actively edited; this reference describes that commit. Licence CC BY 4.0. Scope: open.
**Structure:** One Markdown guide in six teaching chapters (Introduction; AI concepts; Decide on approaches; Prepare; Core tasks; Preventing vulnerabilities longer term), then a call to action, acknowledgements, a 141-entry keyed bibliography and the licence; 46 multiple-choice quizzes close most sections, and 16 figures (15 illustrations, one chart) sit in the text. Cited here as (§ "Section heading").

## Author's Thesis (condensed)

The guide is for developers finding and fixing unintentional vulnerabilities in software they are responsible for, and for security researchers helping them; it states general principles it expects to outlast any one tool, and leaves out building AI systems, AI-specific software risks, general secure coding and malicious software (§ "Scope of this material"). Its urgency rests on four steps: AI has sped up vulnerability-finding, attackers use that speed, manual closed approaches cannot keep up, and humans still matter if they know how to apply AI (§ "Why this is important"). Against the urgency it sets continuity: the fundamental principles of secure development have not changed, AI mostly finds the same old kinds of vulnerabilities, and a project that works hard to find and fix them becomes increasingly hard to find more in, even with AI (§ "What hasn’t changed"; § "Good news: Long-term potential for eliminating nearly all vulnerabilities").

The method follows the chapters: decide on approaches, prepare (the AI, threat models, sandbox, logging, code and documentation, CI/CD, dependency updates), carry out the core tasks (identify, handle external findings, deduplicate, validate, triage, fix, verify, report, release, repeat), and prevent (limit vibe coding, evaluate every merge/pull request, secure by design and by default, harden) (§ "Overview"; § "Call to action"). Across it run a few structural rules: separate finding from validation, make the verifier independent, sandbox rather than rely on text instructions, enforce gates and invariants outside the AI, turn findings into deterministic checks, and keep humans accountable, since "humans are always responsible for what an AI does" [V] (§ "Need for sandboxes"). The guide dates its own evidence: models, services and statistics reflect what was known when it was last reviewed (§ "No endorsement intended").

## Why Now, and What Has Not Changed

The guide argues AI has collapsed the cost of finding vulnerabilities, finds far more of them, turns them into exploits and chains quickly, and has put sophisticated attacks within reach of far more attackers [BT] (§ "AI is accelerating vulnerability-finding"). It reports that the interval between disclosure and exploitation has shrunk from months to days or hours and, by 2025, inverted, with exploitation on average before patches are released [BT] (§ "Attack speed is accelerating"). Slow manual processes are failing, a released patch is itself a roadmap to the bug, hiding source code does not help, and declining to use AI for defence may in some cases be considered negligence [BT] (§ "Manual closed approaches are failing").

Continuity is the counterweight. Least privilege, minimal attack surface, coordinated disclosure and proactive engineering still win; what AI changes is velocity [BT] (§ "What hasn’t changed"). The long view is hopeful: software and its defects are finite, a well-defended project already sees few AI-found bugs, and once vulnerabilities are found and fixed attackers cannot exploit them, though getting there may mean briefly reprioritising everything else [AR] [BT] (§ "Good news: Long-term potential for eliminating nearly all vulnerabilities"). Six terms anchor the rest: attacker, vulnerability, finding ("A finding isn’t a confirmed vulnerability until it’s validated." [V]), exploit, proof of concept or proof of vulnerability, and chaining (§ "Key security terms").

## AI Concepts and Weaknesses

The guide defines its vocabulary: models, frontier models, LLMs, chatbots (which cannot act on their environment), agents (which can, through tools), the *agent harness* that runs a model in a perceive–reason–act–observe loop, and *agent skills* loaded when relevant (§ "Basic AI terminology"). AI is not sentient, though it can simulate intelligence; task horizons are reported to be doubling roughly every seven months [BT] (§ "Basic AI terminology").

Strengths are speed, tool use and tireless parallel work; five weaknesses bear on the task: limited context windows, unsound analysis (no guarantee of finding everything), incorrect results, dependence on training data that is full of vulnerable code, and injection, since an LLM cannot tell commands from content, so repository text should be treated as data, never as authority to widen the agent's task or permissions (§ "Strengths and weaknesses"). Using an external model means trusting its provider's handling of data and its availability, which once failed for reasons outside the provider's control [BT]; local models keep data in-house but are often less capable; licences govern what can be done with a model; specialised small models can outperform larger ones on narrow tasks [BT]; and guardrails built to block attack help can block defenders too, so permissions should be sought before they are needed (§ "Models"). Even "fully autonomous" cyber reasoning systems presume initial human direction and human review of results (§ "Cyber Reasoning System (CRS) history").

## Choosing an Approach

Do not ignore AI or ban AI-assisted reports, since refusing it while facing AI-enabled attackers "can only end one way: compromise" [V]; this is distinct from accepting AI-generated code uncritically (§ "Do not ignore AI"). Do not wait for the best restricted models; start with widely available ones, since the bottleneck is reported to have moved from finding bugs to deciding which to fix first [BT] (§ "Do not wait for access to the best AI models"). Start with simple prompts, then observe and iterate (§ "Do simple things first"). Do not presume AI can fix every vulnerability: reported studies find AI fixes for complex vulnerabilities often fail, add new vulnerabilities, or cover only the example input, with criticisms of one such study also reported; "in many ways AI systems act like junior developers" [V], and complete fixes of complex vulnerabilities are where they are weakest (§ "Do not presume AI can correctly fix all vulnerabilities").

Guiding the AI with a process tends to make it more effective: generic "find bugs" prompts drift, fill context and raise false positives, while narrow scope, adversarial second agents, splitting the bug question from the reachability question, and many parallel narrow tasks reportedly do better [BT] (§ "Why AI tends to be more effective if guided by processes"). The guide lays out several reported pipelines (recon, hunt, validate, gapfill, dedupe, trace, feedback, report; or threat model, sandbox, discovery, verification, triage, patching) [BT], warns that overprescribing can constrain an AI, and notes processes can be human-guided, automated or mixed (§ "How to apply processes for using AI to find and fix vulnerabilities"). Tool benchmarks deserve skepticism, since published results mix definitions and often count unvalidated findings; try a tool on code you know (§ "Challenges of finding and evaluating tools"). Two OpenSSF tools illustrate the range, a simple skill set and a framework for running and ensembling many reasoning systems, with humans still reviewing proposed patches (§ "Scrutineer"; § "OSS-CRS"). Because AI is non-deterministic, run it more than once and repeat until runs reliably come up empty (§ "Run AI multiple times").

## Preparing the AI, Threat Model, Sandbox and Pipeline

Pick tools, possibly several; use cheaper systems for simpler problems but avoid weak or mismatched ones; set reasoning effort fairly high; trim unnecessary output while keeping enough to verify; and treat persistent memory "as another input, not as authoritative truth" [V] (§ "Preparing AI"). Define security requirements, usually as a threat model, because "Neither humans nor AI can determine whether something is a vulnerability without a clear definition for a specific project." [V] At least two threat models apply: one for the development, build and release environment, including the AI, and one for the deployed system; AI can help draft them but its output is not to be taken as truth, and the guide lists AI-era considerations from containment and least privilege to keeping the threat model next to the code (§ "Preparing threat models").

Agents need a sandbox because "all inputs to an AI are simply suggestions" [V] and the guide reports real cases of models breaking out of test environments [BT] (§ "Need for sandboxes"). Match isolation to capability, from reading code up to running proofs of concept; keep credential files out of reach; set execution bounds and record when one ends a run; pin builds; cut network access except to the model; and treat agents as distinct principals with only the permissions their role needs (§ "Implementing sandboxes"). Set a human gate that is "simple, certain, and clear to all participants" [V], never dependent on the AI, with no credential that lets the AI cross it; enforce invariants outside the AI (for example with hooks), audit for indirect bypasses, and keep a kill switch (§ "Establish a human gate and kill switch"). Log AI activity where the AI cannot change it (§ "Preparing AI logging"); improve code and documentation, including an `AGENTS.md` (§ "Preparing the code and documentation"); build a CI/CD pipeline that checks the AI's work, treating task verifiers as part of the trusted computing base and keeping CI to minutes (§ "Preparing CI/CD"); and automate dependency updates, since updating is often safer than proving a vulnerability unexploitable (§ "Preparing dependency updates").

## Identifying, Deduplicating and Validating Findings

A bare "find vulnerabilities" request can work but gives poor coverage; many narrow agents plus deduplication do better [BT] (§ "Identify findings"). Separate discovery from validation, so discovery does not self-censor true positives [BT] (§ "Separate identifying findings from validation"). The guide lists eleven aids to discovery, among them tools, traditional analysers (with AI used to prioritise warnings, never to silently discard them), focus on untrusted input and authentication, clustering past bugs, top lists, the seams between components, invariants across state transitions, important non-security bugs, and configuration and deployment (§ "Helping to identify findings"). Define structured output with provenance, ask for a proof of concept without requiring one, track findings systematically, repeat runs, and record an analysis that did not finish separately from one that found nothing (§ "Helping to identify findings"; § "Managing findings").

Handle external reports as findings, publish a reporting policy that requires validated evidence, and note reported evidence that AI slop can be countered [BT] (§ "Handle external findings"). Deduplicate before and after validation, by root cause [BT] (§ "Deduplicate"). Validation needs a threat model, a validation infrastructure and a stated level of proof, from abnormal behaviour up to a reliable exploit; a mechanism counts as defence in depth only if it is additional, not required; and failing to produce a proof of concept does not prove a false positive [BT] (§ "Defining what a vulnerability is"; § "Defining the proof required"). The verifier should be independent of the discoverer and should try to disprove the finding; agreement among AI reviewers is not proof; a proof of concept must measure the target, trigger on the vulnerable version only, and stay quiet on benign input and on the fixed version [BT] (§ "Tips for validation").

## Triage, Fixing and Verifying Fixes

"Triage is fundamentally a risk decision." [V] It weighs likelihood and impact; AI severity estimates are unreliable, so a human reviews those that matter, and giving the AI the threat model and specific questions first helps; apparently unexploitable defects still deserve fixing because chaining is cheap now (§ "Triage"). Fixing is what makes finding useful, and volume has jumped [BT] (§ "Fix vulnerabilities"). Assign every fix an owner; write a test that fails on the existing code before fixing; fix the root cause and search for variants; give the fixing AI only verified information; prompt for complete, small, reviewable fixes that reuse existing code; and limit unreviewed improvement loops, since reported studies found iterated AI rewrites adding vulnerabilities and regressions [BT] (§ "Fix vulnerabilities", all subsections).

Verify every fix, AI-written or human, first with AI (a new agent probing the patch, variations of the proof of concept) and then with expert humans, who watch for instance-only fixes, duplicated constructs, and invented or wrong dependencies, since "Even very good AI writes vulnerable code." [V] (§ "Verify fixes"; § "Have humans review the fix"). Apply the usual peer review, CI/CD and branch protection (§ "Apply your usual verification processes"). Then turn what was learned into deterministic checks that run on every change, rather than relying on AI to notice the problem again (§ "Turn findings into durable checks").

## Reporting, Releasing and Repeating

Report to external maintainers through their process, with reproducing inputs, tests and a human-reviewed proposed fix, after checking the bug still exists; state the assumed deployment model early, since AIs tend to assume the most permissive one; treat submitting, publishing, merging, deploying and modifying production as approval boundaries enforced in the tool; and follow projects' rules for AI-assisted contributions, under which a human certifies, reviews and takes responsibility [BT] (§ "Reporting to externally maintained projects"). Some laws require reporting actively exploited vulnerabilities to authorities quickly (§ "Reporting to authorities"); users are usually told only once a fix exists (§ "Reporting to users").

Fixes help no one until released and deployed, and "A released fix is also a map to the vulnerability." [V] So develop fixes privately where practical, release fix, release and advisory together for all supported versions, shorten release cycles, make updating easy, and accept updates quickly with automated testing, while "Humans still need to be in control" [V] (§ "Release and deploy"). Apply AI repeatedly, fix systematically, and run deterministic checks plus AI review on every proposed change (§ "Repeated application").

## Preventing Vulnerabilities Longer Term

Finding and fixing is not enough (§ "Preventing vulnerabilities longer term"). Limit vibe coding, meaning AI-generated code no human reviews, wherever results matter for security; where code cannot have a security impact, "vibe coding may be fine" [V]. The guide reports a study in which AI-assisted participants wrote less secure code yet believed it more secure [BT] (§ "Limit vibe coding"). Evaluate every merge/pull request with AI and human review; an agent reviewing untrusted changes gets no secrets or write tokens, the fewest tools, short-lived credentials, output treated as untrusted, and analysis separated from action, because reported attacks have turned such agents against their own repositories [BT] (§ "Evaluate merge/pull requests").

Apply secure by design and secure by default, since most users run the default (§ "Apply secure by design and secure by default"). Harden so that defects are systematically unlikely to become exploitable: prefer reliable mechanisms to friction-based ones, which AI erodes; evaluate the system with hardening disabled and test the hardening itself; and harden the deployed environment, with identity, patching, logging, backups and continuity plans (§ "Harden", all subsections). The guide closes against panic: "It means it’s time to work. Now." [V] (§ "Call to action").

## Key Statistics

All are the guide's reports of outside findings [BT] unless marked as the guide's own.

| Metric | Value | Section |
|---|---|---|
| Disclosure-to-exploitation interval | months (2018) to days (2023); in 2025 exploitation on average before patches | Attack speed is accelerating |
| Complex AI fixes fully correct (one vendor study) | 26.0%; 53.9% unresolved, a new vulnerability, or both; a later review found 86% blocked the supplied exploit, a figure it calls too generous | Do not presume AI can correctly fix all vulnerabilities |
| C/C++ fixes correct (benchmark) | roughly half; best agent 59%; 31% unsolved by any | Do not presume AI can correctly fix all vulnerabilities |
| Findings exploitable with a well-defined threat model | 90 percent | Preparing threat models |
| Static-analysis false positives filtered by agents | over 92% to 6.3%, but 22.25% of real vulnerabilities dismissed | Helping to identify findings |
| Adversarial verifier | roughly halved non-exploitable findings; with a required proof of concept, false positives near zero | Tips for validation |
| AI reviewer consensus | ten AI reviewers endorsed a non-existent flaw; an empirical gate killed about 79% of 171 candidates | Tips for validation |
| Published validation checks rerun | 20 of 30 still fired on the patched version; 7 of 19 negative controls fired on benign input | Tips for validation |
| Iterated AI-only improvement | 37.6% more critical vulnerabilities after five rounds; in infrastructure-as-code repair, 13.8% regressed, gains level off after about three rounds | Approaching fixes |
| Hallucinated packages | at least 5.2% (commercial) and 21.7% (open-source) in 2024-era models; 4.62% to 6.10% in a newer replication | Have humans review the fix |
| CI time for most projects (the guide's own) | "total minutes, at worst an hour" | Preparing CI/CD |

## Key Connections

- The guide cites about 140 outside works by its own bibliography keys: AI-lab, vendor and browser-team reports, agency and industry guidance, OS-kernel project documentation, practitioner posts, a private interview, and many papers listed by arXiv link with no venue. None was read for this reference; their findings are the guide's report [BT].
- It points to the OWASP ASVS chapters as a verification checklist for web applications and to an OWASP top-ten list for agentic applications [BT] (§ "Helping to identify findings").
- It links companion OpenSSF and Linux Foundation material, including a companion document by the guide's lead author (§ "Scope of this material"; § "Preparing the code and documentation").
- Records one disagreement among its sources: whether more prescriptive prompts worsen discovery, while "all the sources we’ve seen agree that providing a threat model and tools is vital" [V] (§ "Helping to identify findings").

## Signature Contrarian Positions

1. Ignoring or banning AI, including AI-assisted reports, ends in compromise (§ "Do not ignore AI").
2. Do not wait for the best restricted models; start now (§ "Do not wait for access to the best AI models").
3. Do not depend on text commands alone to limit an AI; gates and invariants live outside it (§ "Need for sandboxes"; § "Establish a human gate and kill switch").
4. Self-review and AI consensus are not validation; empirical confirmation is (§ "Tips for validation").
5. Do not rely on rerunning AI to catch a known problem; make it a deterministic check (§ "Turn findings into durable checks").
6. Faster patching alone does not solve the patch-diffing problem; reduce the supply of bugs (§ "Release and deploy").
7. Friction-based hardening, and ASLR alone, are weak against AI; use reliable mechanisms (§ "Harden to counter chaining").
8. Do not panic; work (§ "Call to action").
